sentences.text: Researchers utilized a mouse model of Saethre-Chotzen syndrome to track skull and brain morphology from birth until two weeks of age. While control mice maintained an open front skull seam, every mutant mouse exhibited complete closure by day 14, initially presenting with a shortened front-to-back width that evolved into a distinct short-and-wide head shape by day 7.

This abnormal head shape was associated with the widening of specific back-of-the-head skull seams, while the brains of these mutants bulged upward and backward between days 7 and 14, occurring slightly later than the cranial changes. The authors propose that this brain bulging results from pressure exerted by the fused front seam, potentially driving the separation of the posterior seams.

Ultimately, the widened back skull seams reverted to normal dimensions through the extra growth of a specific bone in that region. The authors conclude that this compensatory bone growth restores skull size, though the study remains limited to this specific animal model.
